poem.label: The poem’s own voice
poem.note: The voice that belongs to no named character. It opens the poem (1–7), describes the room at the start of Part II, introduces Madame Sosostris (43–46), speaks the lines on the drowned Phlebas in Part IV and the opening of Part V (322–330), brings on the thunder (396–400), and answers each DA (402–410, 412–417, 419–423). Lines 1–7 are given here to this voice and lines 8–18 to Marie. The division is this edition’s, and it can be argued against: the “us” of line 5 returns at line 8, and the critic Cleanth Brooks (1939) read lines 1–18 as one voice.

marie.label: Marie
marie.note: A woman remembering a summer: coffee and talk in the Hofgarten in Munich, and a sled ride in the mountains as a child with her cousin the archduke. Lines 8–18, except the sentence of German at line 12, which this edition gives to another speaker. Eliot had met Countess Marie Larisch (1858–1940), a niece of the Empress Elisabeth of Austria, and the sledding story came word for word from her conversation; her memoir My Past (1913) has the archduke who was her cousin, the mountains where one feels free and the winters in the south.

stranger.label: A voice in German
stranger.note: Line 12, one sentence, spoken by a woman (the German is feminine, “Russin”): “I am not Russian at all, I come from Lithuania, a real German.” The poem does not say who speaks it; giving it to a second speaker is a reading.

prophet.label: The prophet
prophet.note: Lines 19–30: a voice speaking as the Old Testament prophets do, addressing its hearer as “Son of man,” the words with which God addresses Ezekiel (Eliot’s note cites Ezekiel 2:1), and offering the shade of the red rock. Eliot’s note on line 23 cites Ecclesiastes; “the shadow of this red rock” has been linked to Isaiah 32:2.

sailor.label: Wagner’s sailor
sailor.note: The young sailor singing from the masthead at the opening of Wagner’s opera Tristan und Isolde, Act I: lines 31–34.

lover.label: The one who could not speak
lover.note: The one who came back from the hyacinth garden and could not speak. Lines 37–41: “I could not / Speak, and my eyes failed.”

shepherd.label: Wagner’s shepherd
shepherd.note: Line 42: the shepherd in Tristan und Isolde, Act III, who has looked out for Isolde’s ship and reports the sea desolate and empty.

sosostris.label: Madame Sosostris
sosostris.note: The fortune-teller (the poem’s word is clairvoyante), reading the cards. Lines 43–46 introduce her in the poem’s own voice; she speaks from the middle of line 46 (“Here, said she”) to line 59.

walker.label: The walker in the City of London
walker.note: The “I” of three passages, read here as one voice: the crowd on London Bridge and the meeting with Stetson (60–76), Mr. Eugenides, whose invitation is reported (207–214), and the music along the Strand and the bar in Lower Thames Street (257–265); at 257 he speaks a line from Shakespeare’s The Tempest, spoken there by Ferdinand, the prince who sits on the shore believing his father drowned.

she.label: The woman with bad nerves
she.note: Lines 111–114, 117, 119, 121–123, 126 and 131–134, printed in quotation marks, unlike the man’s. The quotation marks are usually taken to mean that she speaks aloud.

he.label: The man who does not answer
he.note: Lines 115–116, 118, 120, 124–125, 127–130 and 135–138, printed without quotation marks, which is usually read as meaning that he does not speak aloud. Some of his replies are other people’s words: the playwrights Webster (118) and Middleton (137–138), both cited in Eliot’s notes; the song of the spirit Ariel in Shakespeare’s The Tempest (125); and the song “That Shakespearian Rag” of 1912 (128–130).
sources: Buck, Ruby and Stamper, "That Shakespearian Rag" (1912)

pub.label: Lil’s friend, in the pub
pub.note: A woman in a pub, telling what she said to her friend Lil about Lil’s husband Albert, home from the army. Lines 139–171, interrupted by the publican’s call.

publican.label: The publican
publican.note: The landlord calling closing time: HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME, at lines 141, 152, 165, 168 and 169.

ophelia.label: Ophelia
ophelia.note: Line 172: Ophelia’s good night in Hamlet (Act IV, scene 5), as she goes out, mad. Her drowning is reported two scenes later.

fisher.label: The fisher on the bank
fisher.note: The speaker by the river in Part III, lines 173–198, who repeats the refrain of the Elizabethan poet Edmund Spenser, “Sweet Thames, run softly”, and fishes in the dull canal behind the gashouse. He speaks partly in others’ lines: Spenser’s (176, 183–184), Psalm 137 at 182 (“By the waters of Babylon we sat down and wept,” in the Prayer Book’s wording), and at 191–192, as Eliot’s note on line 192 says, those of Ferdinand, the prince in Shakespeare’s The Tempest who sits on the shore mourning a father he believes drowned. That he is the Fisher King of the Grail legend, the wounded king whose land lies waste with him, is the reading of the critic Cleanth Brooks (1939), among others; Eliot’s notes name the Fisher King at lines 46 and 425.

song.label: Songs quoted
song.note: Lines 199–202: the ballad about Mrs Porter (199–201), which Eliot’s note on line 199 says was reported to him from Sydney, Australia, and the last line of the French poet Paul Verlaine’s sonnet “Parsifal”, on children singing in the dome (202). The rag at lines 128–130 is given to the man who does not answer.

nightingale.label: The nightingale
nightingale.note: Lines 203–206: the nightingale’s song as the Elizabethan poets wrote it, “jug jug” and “Tereu,” calling on Tereus, the king who raped Philomel; her story is told at lines 99–103, and “So rudely forc’d” repeats line 100.

tiresias.label: Tiresias
tiresias.note: Lines 215–251 and 253–256: the blind seer of Thebes in the Metamorphoses of the Roman poet Ovid, once a woman for seven years, who says he “can see” the typist’s evening and has “foresuffered all.” Eliot’s note on line 218, which quotes Ovid, calls him “a mere spectator and not indeed a ‘character’” and yet “the most important personage in the poem, uniting all the rest.”

typist.label: The typist
typist.note: Line 252, her only words, in quotation marks: what the poem calls her “one half-formed thought.”

thames.label: The Thames-daughters, together
thames.note: The three Thames-daughters, as Eliot’s note calls them, singing together: lines 266–291. His note says that from line 292 to 306 they speak in turn. The refrain “Weialala leia” is the Rhine-daughters’ from Wagner’s Götterdämmerung, Act III, which the note cites.

thames1.label: First Thames-daughter
thames1.note: Highbury, Richmond and Kew: lines 292–295. Eliot’s note sends the reader to Dante’s Purgatorio, canto V, and quotes the line of La Pia, one of the dead there: “Siena mi fe’, disfecemi Maremma,” Siena made me, Maremma unmade me.

ascetic.label: Augustine and the Buddha
ascetic.note: Lines 307–311: the Confessions of St Augustine, the fourth-century bishop (307 and 309–310, beginning “To Carthage then I came”), set beside the Buddha’s Fire Sermon (308 and 311, “Burning”). Eliot’s note calls them “two representatives of eastern and western asceticism” and says that setting them side by side “is not an accident.”

pilgrim.label: The pilgrim on the road
pilgrim.note: The voice in the mountains without water, asking who walks beside you: lines 331–366.

seer.label: The one who sees the cities fall
seer.note: Lines 367–395, from “What is that sound high in the air” to “Bringing rain.” Eliot’s note on lines 367–377, where the hooded hordes swarm, cites Blick ins Chaos (1920), essays on Dostoevsky and the downfall of Europe by the German novelist Hermann Hesse.

thunder.label: The thunder
thunder.note: “DA,” at lines 401, 411 and 418. Eliot’s note on line 402 says the fable of the thunder’s meaning is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, one of the Hindu scriptures.

fisherking.label: The Fisher King
fisherking.note: Lines 424–426: “I sat upon the shore / Fishing, with the arid plain behind me.” Eliot’s note on line 425 refers to the chapter on the Fisher King, the wounded king whose land lies waste with him, in Jessie L. Weston’s book on the Grail legend, From Ritual to Romance; the poem does not name the speaker.
sources: Weston, From Ritual to Romance, ch. IX

fragments.label: The fragments
fragments.note: Lines 427–432, line by line: the nursery rhyme “London Bridge is falling down” (427); Dante’s Purgatorio, canto XXVI (428); the Latin poem Pervigilium Veneris, and then “O swallow swallow”, from the song in The Princess, a poem by Tennyson (429); the sonnet “El Desdichado” by the French poet Gérard de Nerval (430); the poem’s own line, “These fragments I have shored against my ruins” (431); and The Spanish Tragedy, the Elizabethan play by Thomas Kyd (432). Eliot’s notes give the sources at 428, 429, 430 and 432.
sources: Gomme, Traditional Games, vol. I, pp. 333–349
Tennyson, The Princess, the song "O Swallow, Swallow"

upanishad.label: The Upanishad
upanishad.note: The poem’s last two lines, 433–434. Eliot’s notes translate the three words as “Give, sympathise, control” and give their source as the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, one of the Hindu scriptures; “Shantih,” repeated three times, is “a formal ending to an Upanishad,” for which “The Peace which passeth understanding” is, his note says, “a feeble translation.”
